title: A notebook
hookLine: keep your rule in one place: Pascal kept the record of his night of fire sewn into his coat
tomorrow: the alarm goes off. what reaches you before your feet hit the floor?

cards: A scrap of parchment. After the scientist and writer Blaise Pascal died, a servant noticed something stiff in the lining of his coat. Sewn inside was a folded parchment, with a paper copy.
His family learned he had carried it for years, unpicking it and sewing it into each new coat he wore. Nobody had known. On it was a date and an hour, late at night.
And then, as a heading, one word: Fire.

teach.b: Under it, in short broken lines, Pascal wrote down the night that changed him.

teach.h: NOT THE GOD OF THE PHILOSOPHERS.
teach.b: God of Abraham, God of Isaac, God of Jacob, not of the philosophers and scholars. Certainty. Certainty.
Joy, joy, joy, tears of joy. It's called his Memorial. Here's the teaching inside it.

Pascal was a brilliant mathematician, and what met him that night wasn't a proof. It was, in his words, the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, the living God of the Bible, met in person, as Christian faith holds God can be.
And he didn't trust himself to remember it.
So he wrote it down, once, in one place, and kept that place against his body. That's what a notebook is for.
This whole stretch has been building a rule: my own, a little rule, five words, my why, already here, one gap, small and real, my honest path. Scattered, they fade.

Kept together, in one notebook you can find, they become something you can return to on the morning you've forgotten all of it. Pascal's page was small enough to sew into a coat. Yours can be small too.
Tomorrow, the daily practice begins, at the very top of the day.

how: Pascal's Memorial is printed alongside his Pensées; some people who keep a rule of life write it in one notebook and reread it.

o: a diary where you record every feeling you have
a planner that tracks your work tasks and deadlines
one place where your written rule lives, kept close

p: the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob
he sewed the page in again

s: Pascal published his Memorial so others could read about his night
nobody knew of it until a servant found it sewn in his coat after he died.
the Memorial calls God the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, not of the philosophers
the mathematician met not a proof but, in his words, the living God.

games.q: your friend keeps her goals in four apps, two journals and a sticky note. she can never find them when she needs them. what fits today's lesson?
o: put the rule in one place she'll keep close, the way Pascal kept his page.
add one more app, so the goals are everywhere she looks.
stop writing goals down; a rule should live only in your head.
games.why: Pascal wrote his night down once and carried that page in every coat. one place you can return to beats many you can't find.

practice: Take a notebook, any notebook, and write on its first page by hand: my rule.
Under it, copy the lines from these foundations that you want to keep, five words, my why, one gap, small and real, my honest path, in your own handwriting. Leave the rest of the page empty for now.

carryVoice: Keep this: one notebook, kept close like Pascal's page in the coat. The foundations are laid.
